title: Plurals and possessives
blurb: Form any plural, regular or irregular, and put the possessive apostrophe in exactly the right place.
question: A hospital sign reads, “Visitor's must check in at the nurses station before entering the childrens' ward.” Every apostrophe is in the wrong place. How do you fix each one, and how do you tell a plural from a possessive on the TEAS?

teach.h: More than one vs belonging to
teach.body: Formally, a plural noun names more than one person, place or thing (nurses, children), and a possessive noun shows ownership or a close relationship (the nurse's badge, the children's ward). Plain English: plurals almost never take an apostrophe; possessives always do. The TEAS tests both: spelling the plural correctly, then deciding whether the apostrophe goes before or after the s.

head: Word ends in
Rule
Examples
rows: s, ss, sh, ch, x, z
teach.caption: Exceptions take only s: roofs, chiefs, beliefs, chefs, proofs; photos, pianos, radios, memos, zoos.

head: Type
Examples
rows: child, children; person, people; tooth, teeth; mouse, mice
deer, sheep, fish, series, species, aircraft
diagnosis, diagnoses; analysis, analyses; crisis, crises
bacterium, bacteria; criterion, criteria; datum, data
nucleus, nuclei; stimulus, stimuli; vertebra, vertebrae
teach.caption: Compound nouns pluralize the main word. Numbers and capital abbreviations add s with no apostrophe: 1990s, RNs. Some of these nouns also have an accepted English plural (funguses, vertebras), so test items target forms that are plainly wrong, such as diagnosises.
Always form the owner first, then add the apostrophe. Never put an apostrophe inside the word (childrens').
Read it aloud: nurse's, nurses and nurses' all sound alike, so the spelling must carry the meaning.

teach.body: Joint ownership puts the apostrophe on the last name only: Maria and Lee's clinic (one clinic). Separate ownership marks each name: Maria's and Lee's cars (two sets). A compound noun takes the apostrophe on its last word: my sister-in-law's car. Time works like ownership: a week's pay, two weeks' notice. Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: its, yours, hers, ours, theirs, whose.

Marcus Reed, a nursing applicant, rewrites: “Visitors must check in at the nurses' station before entering the children's ward.” Visitors is a plain plural (no ownership), so no apostrophe. The station belongs to many nurses, a plural ending in s, so the apostrophe follows the s. Children is already plural without s, so it takes 's.

rows.label: The patients' rooms are on floor 2.

teach.note: Ask “does anything belong to it?” If not, the word needs no apostrophe.

teach.text: The TEAS traps: an apostrophe in a plain plural (“patient's” for patients), the apostrophe on the wrong side (“childrens'”, “nurse's station” for many nurses), adding -es to a Latin plural (“criterias”), and an apostrophe in its, yours or theirs. Possessive pronouns are already possessive.

items: Plurals: + s, + es after s/sh/ch/x/z, y to ies after a consonant, many f/fe to ves.
Learn the irregular and Latin/Greek plurals: children, teeth, criteria, diagnoses, nuclei, vertebrae.
Possessive: singular + 's; plural ending in s + '; plural not ending in s + 's.
Joint ownership marks the last name only; compounds mark the last word.
Never use an apostrophe for a plain plural or in its, yours, hers, ours, theirs or whose.

summary: You can now form regular, irregular and Latin/Greek plurals and place the possessive apostrophe correctly for singular, plural, joint and compound owners. You can also reject apostrophes in plain plurals and possessive pronouns.

A.q: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: “The admissions committee listed three ___ for selecting applicants.”
options: criterion
criterias
criteria
criteriae
A.why: Criterion is singular; its plural is criteria.

whyNot.0: Criterion is the singular form, but the sentence needs three.
whyNot.1: Criteria is already plural, so adding -s makes a double plural.
whyNot.3: The -ae ending belongs to Latin nouns ending in -a (vertebrae); criterion follows -on to -a.

A.q: Which sentence uses the correct plural forms?
options: The chefs placed the knives on the shelves.
The cheves placed the knives on the shelves.
The chefs placed the knifes on the shelves.
The chefs placed the knives on the shelfs.
A.why: Chef is an exception that takes s (chefs); knife becomes knives and shelf becomes shelves.

whyNot.1: Chef is one of the f exceptions that simply adds s: chefs.
whyNot.2: Knife changes fe to ves: knives.
whyNot.3: Shelf changes f to ves: shelves.

A.q: Twelve patients share one lounge. Which phrase correctly shows that the lounge belongs to all of them?
options: the patient's lounge
the patients' lounge
the patients lounge
the patients's lounge
A.why: Patients is a plural ending in s, so the possessive adds only an apostrophe: patients'.

whyNot.0: Patient's is singular possessive: a lounge belonging to one patient.
whyNot.2: Without an apostrophe, patients is a plain plural and shows no ownership.
whyNot.3: A plural ending in s takes only an apostrophe, not 's.

B.q: Which sentence uses possessive forms correctly?
options: The childrens' ward and the women's clinic share a lobby.
The children's ward and the womens' clinic share a lobby.
The childrens ward and the women's clinic share a lobby.
The children's ward and the women's clinic share a lobby.
B.why: Children and women are plurals that do not end in s, so each takes 's.

whyNot.0: Children is already plural, so the apostrophe goes before the added s: children's.
whyNot.1: Women is already plural, so the apostrophe goes before the added s: women's.
whyNot.2: Childrens with no apostrophe is not a word; the possessive is children's.

B.q: Which sentence spells every plural correctly?
options: The cafeteria posted photoes of the potatoes and tomatoes.
The cafeteria posted photos of the potatoes and tomatoes.
The cafeteria posted photos of the potatos and tomatoes.
The cafeteria posted photos of the potatoes and tomatos.
B.why: Photo is an exception that adds s; potato and tomato add es.

whyNot.0: Photo is one of the o exceptions that adds only s: photos.
whyNot.2: Potato is consonant + o and takes es: potatoes.
whyNot.3: Tomato is consonant + o and takes es: tomatoes.

B.q: Which sentence uses possessive pronouns correctly?
options: The clinic updated its hours, so the choice is yours.
The clinic updated it's hours, so the choice is yours.
The clinic updated its hours, so the choice is your's.
The clinic updated its' hours, so the choice is yours.
B.why: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: its, yours.

whyNot.1: It's means “it is,” which makes no sense before hours.
whyNot.2: Yours is a possessive pronoun and never takes an apostrophe.
whyNot.3: Its' is not a word; the possessive pronoun is its.

C.q: Dana and Omar own one clinic together. Which sentence correctly shows their shared ownership?
options: Dana's and Omar's clinic opened in May.
Dana and Omars' clinic opened in May.
Dana and Omar's clinic opened in May.
Dana's and Omar clinic opened in May.
C.why: For joint ownership, only the last name takes the possessive: Dana and Omar's clinic.

whyNot.0: Marking both names shows separate ownership, which does not fit one shared clinic.
whyNot.1: Omar is singular, so the possessive is Omar's, not Omars'.
whyNot.3: In joint ownership the apostrophe goes on the last name, not the first.

C.q: Which sentence uses the correct plural of the compound noun?
options: Both mother-in-laws attended the graduation.
Both mothers-in-laws attended the graduation.
Both mother-in-law's attended the graduation.
Both mothers-in-law attended the graduation.
C.why: A compound noun pluralizes its main word: mother becomes mothers, giving mothers-in-law.

whyNot.0: The main word is mother, not law, so the s goes on mother.
whyNot.1: Only the main word is made plural; laws should stay law.
whyNot.2: An apostrophe shows possession, not a plural.

options: After two weeks' notice, the RNs moved to the night shift.
After two week's notice, the RNs moved to the night shift.
After two weeks' notice, the RN's moved to the night shift.
After two weeks notice, the RN's moved to the night shift.
C.why: Weeks is a plural ending in s, so its possessive is weeks'. RNs is a plain plural with no apostrophe.

whyNot.1: Two weeks is plural, so the apostrophe goes after the s: weeks'.
whyNot.2: Capital abbreviations form plurals with s alone: RNs.
whyNot.3: Weeks needs a possessive apostrophe, and RNs needs none.

reteach.title: The apostrophe is a name tag
reteach.question: Think of an apostrophe as a name tag stuck on an owner. Where do you stick the tag when there is one owner, a crowd of owners, or no owner at all?

blocks.h: Find the owner, then tag it
blocks.body: First, write the owner exactly as it is: nurse (one), nurses (a crowd), children (a crowd without s). Then stick the tag on the end. One nurse: nurse's. A crowd already ending in s: just the tag, nurses'. A crowd without s: tag plus s, children's. If nobody owns anything (“the nurses left”), there is no tag at all.

steps.label: Owner?
steps.sub: If nothing is owned, no apostrophe

blocks.text: Pronouns wear their own built-in tag: its, yours, theirs and whose never get an apostrophe. It's always means “it is” or “it has.”

explain.body: Add s to most nouns. Add es after s, ss, sh, ch, x or z. Consonant + y becomes ies; vowel + y just adds s (attorneys). Many f/fe words become ves (leaves), but roofs, chiefs and beliefs only add s.

test.q: Which word is the correct plural of its singular form?
options: attornies
quizzes
wishs
babys
test.why: Quiz ends in z, so it adds es, and the single z doubles: quizzes.

whyNot.0: Attorney ends in vowel + y, so it just adds s: attorneys.
whyNot.2: Wish ends in sh, so it adds es: wishes.
whyNot.3: Baby ends in consonant + y, so y changes to ies: babies.

explain.body: Some plurals change the word itself (tooth, teeth; person, people), some do not change (deer, species), and Latin/Greek nouns use their own endings: -is to -es, -um to -a, -us to -i, -a to -ae.

test.q: Which pair shows a correct singular and plural?
options: diagnosis, diagnosises
thesis, thesises
bacterium, bacteriums
vertebra, vertebrae
test.why: Vertebra follows the Latin -a to -ae pattern: vertebrae.

explain.body: Singular owner: add 's (the doctor's orders). Plural owner ending in s: add ' only (the doctors' lounge). Plural owner not ending in s: add 's (people's choice).

test.q: Which phrase correctly shows the orders written by a single doctor?
options: the doctors' order's
the doctors' orders
the doctor's orders
the doctors orders
test.why: One doctor is a singular owner, so add 's: doctor's. Orders is a plain plural.

whyNot.0: This makes doctor plural and puts an apostrophe in the plain plural orders.
whyNot.1: Doctors' shows orders from several doctors, not one.
whyNot.3: Doctors with no apostrophe is a plain plural and shows no ownership.

explain.body: Possessive pronouns are already possessive: its, yours, hers, ours, theirs, whose. The apostrophe forms are contractions: it's (it is), who's (who is).

test.q: Which sentence uses whose and hers correctly?
options: Who's coat is this, and is it her's?
Whose coat is this, and is it hers?
Whose coat is this, and is it her's?
Who's coat is this, and is it hers?
test.why: Whose shows ownership and hers is a possessive pronoun; neither takes an apostrophe.

whyNot.0: Who's means “who is,” and hers never takes an apostrophe.
whyNot.2: Hers is a possessive pronoun and never takes an apostrophe.
whyNot.3: Who's means “who is”; ownership needs whose.
